title: CasNano: An ultracompact CRISPR-Cas12f with a GC-rich PAM for epigenome editing with therapeutic potential.
authors: Kim, Dongkyeong; Huang, Chia-Wei; Pan, Richard; Qian, Junming; Wu, Xuebing; Devinsky, Orrin; Tsai, Yi-Ting; Liu, Shawn
abstract: Clinical use of CRISPR-Cas proteins for genome engineering is constrained by their large size, limiting in vivo delivery. To address this, we engineered an ultracompact and versatile platform from a minimally active, 400-amino acid Cas12f protein from Blautia lenta. A multi-stage strategy of structure-guided protein mutagenesis and systematic single guide RNA (sgRNA) optimization transformed BlCas12f into a "CasNano" as a potent genome targeting tool for mammalian cells. When a catalytically dead CasNano (dCasNano) is fused to a VPR domain, it activates endogenous genes with an efficiency and specificity comparable or superior to the benchmark SpCas9 system for the guide RNAs (gRNAs) and loci tested under equal-mass plasmid transfection; as editor expression was not quantified and stoichiometric differences would, in any case, preclude equivalent normalization, these comparisons describe functional output rather than intrinsic activity. We established the platform's versatility for bidirectional epigenetic editing by fusing dCasNano to a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT3A) for gene silencing or a dioxygenase (TET1) for gene activation. TET1-mediated reactivation persisted for 5 months in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), whereas DNMT3A-deposited methylation was not retained at 2 weeks in a dividing reporter line. CasNano's small size and distinct CCN PAM sequence highlight its potential for future therapeutic applications constrained by viral delivery cargo capacity.

title: Oocyst wall protein EtOWP6 is critical for sporocyst formation and developmental progression in Eimeria tenella.
authors: Jia, Liushu; Wang, Jinwen; Wang, Qingjie; Wang, Lu; Zhu, Shunhai; Zhao, Qiping; Wu, Shanbo; Han, Wenqi; Bai, Jaiyu; Zhao, Fanghe; Yu, Yu; Han, Hongyu; Dong, Hui
abstract: Transmission of apicomplexan parasites-including Eimeria, Toxoplasma, and Cryptosporidium-relies on the environmentally resilient oocyst wall, a bilayered structure whose integrity is maintained by cysteine-rich oocyst wall proteins (OWPs). Yet the functional roles of these conserved proteins remain poorly defined. Here, we characterize EtOWP6, a conserved OWP in Eimeria tenella, the causative agent of avian coccidiosis. Immunofluorescence reveals that EtOWP6 localizes specifically to wall-forming bodies and oocyst/sporocyst walls during sexual development. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout demonstrates that EtOWP6 is essential for sporocyst formation, with deficient parasites exhibiting malformed sporocysts, developmental arrest in vitro, and an in vivo reduction in oocyst output exceeding 85%. The knockout strain is highly attenuated yet retains partial immunogenicity. Transcriptomic analysis reveals that EtOWP6 deletion induces widespread transcriptional reprogramming, disrupting genes critical for developmental regulation and oocyst wall biogenesis. Our findings establish EtOWP6 as a critical regulator coupling structural integrity with developmental progression in Eimeria, and more broadly, highlight OWPs as conserved targets for transmission-blocking interventions across apicomplexan parasites.

title: Optimisation and mechanistic characterization of a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor in pancreatic cancer cells.
authors: Wu, Yi-Wen; Yang, Chun-Lin; Fang-Chin, Yu-Ting; Yeh, Yun-Hsuan; Chen, Bor-Jiun; Sung, Tzu-Ying; Chu, Jung-Chun; Lin, Tony Eight; Yen, Shih-Chung; Hsieh, Jui-Hua; Huang, Sing-Han; Chu, Cheng-Ying; Yang, Kai-Chien; Hsu, Kai-Cheng; Pan, Shiow-Lin
journal: Journal of enzyme inhibition and medicinal chemistry
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a lethal malignancy with limited targeted therapeutic options. Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinase 4 (MAP4K4) has been implicated in PDAC progression, but the development of effective MAP4K4 inhibitors requires further improvement in potency, selectivity, and mechanistic characterisation. We previously identified F389-0746 as a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor with anti-cancer activity in pancreatic cancer. Here, we used the F389-0746 scaffold to guide the selection and evaluation of benzoxazine-based analogs, followed by biochemical, structural, selectivity, and cellular characterisation of the most potent analogue. Among the identified analogs, F389-0736 showed the strongest MAP4K4 inhibitory activity, with an IC(50) value of 44.0 nM, representing an approximately threefold improvement over F389-0746. Docking and structure-activity relationship analyses identified key binding interactions that support the enhanced potency of F389-0736 within the MAP4K4 binding pocket. Kinase profiling further demonstrated the selectivity of F389-0736 for MAP4K4 across the tested kinase panel. CETSA further demonstrated F389-0736-induced thermal stabilisation of MAP4K4, supporting intracellular target engagement. In pancreatic cancer cells, F389-0736 suppressed TAK1, JNK, and p38 phosphorylation and significantly reduced cell viability and proliferation, with IC(50) and GI(50) values of 4.41-4.65 muM and 4.03-5.12 muM, respectively. F389-0736 also inhibited clonogenic growth and induced sub-G1 accumulation with activation of apoptotic signalling. RNA sequencing identified 398 differentially expressed genes and revealed enrichment of inflammatory and stress response pathways, programmed cell death programs, oncogenic signalling perturbation, and metabolic reprogramming. These findings identify F389-0736 as a potent and selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor and support its use as a chemical probe and lead scaffold for investigating MAP4K4-dependent signalling and therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

title: HLA-Engineered iPSC-Derived Mesenchymal Stromal Cells for the Treatment of Osteoarthritis in Mice.
authors: Wei, Ze; Gan, Tian; Liang, Annan; Liu, Su; Hao, Jing; Zou, Wei; Li, Lun; Mu, Xuemeng; Han, Huitian; Ma, Wenjing; Xing, Jinyi; Wei, Yifan; Fan, Hao; Liu, Lijin; Liu, Fei; Zheng, Zhifa; Wu, Zhihong; Zhao, Lina
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is one of the most prevalent degenerative joint diseases, and there is no approved pharmacological therapy that can reliably reverse cartilage degeneration or restore cartilage structure. Allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have shown therapeutic potential for OA, but inflammatory conditions can enhance HLA expression and increase allogeneic immune recognition risk. Here, we generated B2M and CIITA double-knockout induced pluripotent stem cells (dKO-iPSCs) using CRISPR/Cas9 and subsequently differentiated them into dKO-iMSCs. B2M/CIITA double-knockout did not affect iPSC pluripotency, karyotype, or teratoma formation. dKO-iMSCs retained characteristic MSC phenotypes, exhibited greater proliferative capacity than tissue-derived MSCs, and could be expanded to passage 18. Notably, HLA-ABC and HLA-DR expression remained undetectable in dKO-iMSCs even after IFN-gamma stimulation. In co-culture assays with PHA-L-stimulated allogeneic PBMCs, dKO-iMSCs suppressed PBMC and T-cell proliferation as effectively as wild-type iMSCs, indicating preservation of their immunomodulatory activity. Intra-articular administration of dKO-iMSCs significantly reduced cartilage degeneration in the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse model of OA. The treatment showed greater therapeutic efficacy than wild-type iMSCs and tissue-derived MSCs and did not cause evident systemic organ toxicity. Single-cell RNA sequencing of BM-MSCs and dKO-iMSCs after in vitro IFN-gamma stimulation revealed enhanced extracellular matrix-associated cell-cell communication and markedly reduced IL1B expression in dKO-iMSCs, indicating a less pro-inflammatory and more matrix-supportive cellular state under inflammatory conditions. Collectively, B2M/CIITA double-knockout enables sustained reduction in HLA expression while preserving the MSC phenotype and immunomodulatory activity, and enhances the therapeutic efficacy of iMSCs in the mouse OA model, providing a potential strategy for developing iPSC-derived MSCs with reduced HLA expression for allogeneic cell therapy.

title: Disabling COMPASS Promoter Licensing Shifts HDAC-Inhibited Gastric Cancer Toward Sustained Transcriptional Suppression During Recovery.
authors: Song, Jintian; Yu, Hui; Jiang, Jianping; Jiang, Zhihui; Hong, Zhongshi; Zhang, Xu; Chen, Luchuan; Wei, Shenghong; Wang, Yi
abstract: Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) broadly increase chromatin acetylation but have limited and variable activity in solid tumors. To define the epigenetic buffering axis that sustains promoter output during HDAC inhibition in gastric cancer. We integrated pharmacologic profiling across a molecularly diverse gastric cancer panel with an epigenetic-focused pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screening library, domain-resolved genetic perturbation, structure-guided WIN-pocket targeting, CCK8 time-course proliferation assays, and pulse-washout clonogenic recovery assays. Chromatin and transcriptional consequences were interrogated by assessing COMPASS integrity and chromatin association, promoter-proximal H3K4me3 dynamics, data-derived ATAC-seq accessibility, and transcriptional output. WDR5 abundance and baseline H3K4me3 levels were associated with sensitivity to combined HDAC and WDR5 WIN-pocket inhibition. Multiple orthogonal approaches identified the WDR5 WIN pocket as a key interface supporting chromatin-associated COMPASS and promoter-proximal H3K4me3 under the tested conditions. WIN-pocket disruption reduced chromatin recovery of COMPASS-associated components and attenuated H3K4me3 at selected growth-linked promoters. This produced a state with elevated H3K27 acetylation, attenuated H3K4me3, and reduced transcriptional output; data-derived ATAC-enriched regions retained a centered accessibility signal, although the mean peak amplitude was lowest in the combination. HDAC inhibitor response is conditioned by promoter licensing via the WDR5-COMPASS H3K4 methylation axis.

title: Starch characteristics distinguish malt from non-malt barley and can be modulated via SBEIIb promoter editing.
authors: Li, Mengdi; He, Peixin; Cai, Kangfeng; Yao, Jie; Huang, Danyin; Zhang, Guoping; Ye, Lingzhen
abstract: Barley is classified as malt or non-malt barley according to its end use, yet the role of starch characteristics in determining malt quality remains poorly understood. In this study, we systematically compared starch content, composition, granule structure, and thermal properties between six malt and six non-malt barley varieties. Compared with non-malt barley, malt barley exhibited significantly higher total starch (TS) content, a lower amylose/amylopectin (Am/Ap) ratio, and a larger area of large starch granules (LSGs), features that may collectively enhance the contact surface for hydrolytic enzymes during mashing. Thermal property analysis further revealed a narrower gelatinization temperature range (R) in malt barley, indicating more synchronized and potentially more efficient starch gelatinization. Based on these distinct starch traits, we employed novel CRISPR/Cas9-mediated editing of the SBEIIb promoter to generate novel barley accessions. The resulting promoter-editing SBEIIb mutants showed a significantly reduced Am/Ap ratio, closely mimicking the altered starch profile potentially relevant to malt quality related traits of elite malt barley varieties, without affecting total starch content or grain morphology. Mechanistically, this compositional shift was associated with altered starch-associated genes expression, demonstrating that targeted promoter modification is a promising strategy for malt barley improvement while avoiding the pleiotropic defects commonly caused by coding-region knockouts. These findings reveal fundamental differences in starch properties between malt and non-malt barley and provide both genetic resources and a feasible breeding strategy for developing superior malt barley cultivars.

title: Programmable synthetic engineering of adaptive microbial cell factories: from amide transforming enzymes to advanced biocatalytic systems.
abstract: Microbial cell factories integrate metabolic engineering, synthetic regulation, protein engineering, and computational design to improve catalytic performance and process robustness. Within this landscape, amide transforming enzymes provide diverse functions ranging from nitrogen metabolism and hydrolysis to covalent protein remodeling. This review examines amidases, asparaginases, glutaminases, nitrilases, nitrile hydratases, acylases, and carbamylases, with particular emphasis on microbial transglutaminase (MTGase). MTGase is distinguished by its ability to catalyze covalent epsilon-(gamma-glutamyl) lysine crosslinking through acyl transfer reactions, enabling protein stabilization, molecular assembly, immobilization, and spatial organization of catalytic systems. This review critically examines the transition from classical amide transforming enzymes toward engineered biocatalytic systems and evaluates how MTGase could be leveraged as a protein level control component in microbial cell factories. Experimental developments in MTGase production, structural and protein engineering, synthetic genetic circuits, CRISPR based regulation, metabolic control, nanobiomaterials, and spatial biocatalysis are evaluated alongside computational approaches including AlphaFold assisted structure prediction, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, machine learning guided mutagenesis, and metabolic modeling. Emphasis is placed on experimentally validated outcomes and current limitations. Key unresolved barriers include intracellular off target crosslinking, proteostatic burden, variable crosslink stoichiometry, limited temporal control of MTGase activity, chassis dependence, and industrial scale up. Where direct evidence is lacking, prospective applications are distinguished from established capabilities and corresponding engineering strategies are proposed. Collectively, this review envisions MTGase as a controllable protein level platform for synthetic biology, while defining the evidence, limitations, and experimental requirements needed for its broader application in microbial biotechnology.

title: Elevational melanism in East African Honey Bees involves a Major-Effect locus.
authors: Mazzoni, Marco; Loidolt, Florian; Kersten, Sonja; Otieno, Mark; Njovu, Henry; Lasway, Julius Vincent; Scheiner, Ricarda; Hasselmann, Martin
abstract: Thermal melanism, whereby darker pigmentation occurs in colder environments, is a widespread pattern, yet its genetic and physiological basis in eusocial insects remains poorly understood. East African honey bees (Apis mellifera) occupy elevational gradients in which highland populations are darker, larger, and more cold tolerant than lowland conspecifics. Here, we integrated population genomics, structural variations, and functional genomics to investigate elevational melanism. We sampled, phenotyped and resequenced 139 workers from five East African mountain systems. A genome wide association study identified 977 Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) significantly associated with abdominal pigmentation, with a single, peak at the ebony ortholog AmEbony on chromosome 1. Allelic variation at AmEbony formed three genetic clusters tracking a continuous pigmentation gradient, and 77 divergent SNPs (DXY = 1) almost perfectly discriminated dark from light bees. Two inversions (r7, r9), previously linked to high elevation adaptation, were detected across additional mountain systems and enriched in dark, highland genomic backgrounds, but did not replace AmEbony as the primary pigmentation locus. CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of AmEbony in A. m. carnica produced darker adults in a qualitative comparison, supporting a conserved role in pigmentation. Head RNA-seq and GENIE3 analysis identified recurrent genotype-associated modules involving oxidoreductase activity and odorant binding. Because population structure covaries with elevation and pigmentation, the GWAS supports AmEbony as a major-effect locus but cannot identify causal variants. Similarly, head-expression data identify molecular changes associated with AmEbony disruption, but cannot establish whether they contribute to pigmentation or whether naturally segregating East African alleles act through the same pathways.

title: Structural basis and rational engineering of a thermophilic Cas13a for robust RNA detection.
authors: Oladeji, Seye J; Gonzalez, Diego H; Deng, Xiangyu; You, Zheng; Zhang, Yuxuan; Golla, Devin A; Smith, Jamie; Zhang, Yi; Gao, Xue; Lillehoj, Peter B; Gao, Yang
abstract: Cas13a enzymes are particularly attractive for nucleic acid detection due to their robust collateral activity. Recently, there has been a surge in the discovery and engineering of thermostable Cas13a proteins for nucleic acid detection. The thermostable Cas13a from Thermoclostridium caenicola (TccCas13a) was identified; however, its native target sensitivity and collateral activity are relatively low and require optimization for molecular diagnostic applications. Here, we report comprehensive biochemical characterization and structure-guided engineering of TccCas13a. Our analyses reveal its intrinsic thermostability, nucleotide substrate preferences, and tolerance to structured target RNA substrates. Rational engineering of the spacer-target RNA binding channel improved target engagement and enabled determination of a 3.13 A cryo-electron microscopy ternary structure. Furthermore, extensive structure-guided engineering of active site-proximal regions yielded a variant with over  approximately 100-fold enhanced target sensitivity and collateral activity across diverse biological matrices. Together, our work provides mechanistic insights and establishes TccCas13a as a platform for next-generation RNA diagnostics.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens identify shared and context-specific regulators of podocyte resistance to oxidative injury.
authors: Zhen, Xuan; Hu, Jiaying; Wang, Xiao; Qing, Jianbo; Wu, Junnan
abstract: Podocyte injury is a convergent driver of glomerular disease progression, yet the genetic determinants that govern podocyte vulnerability to oxidative stress remain incompletely defined. Here, we performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens in differentiated human podocytes exposed to two complementary injury models: Adriamycin (ADR), a clinically relevant inducer of podocyte damage, and hydrogen peroxide (H(2)O(2)), a direct oxidative stress challenge. Human podocytes were transduced with a genome-wide sgRNA library, differentiated under non-permissive conditions and subjected to optimized stress conditions that imposed selective pressure while preserving library complexity. Across five independent replicates per condition, sequencing-based sgRNA profiling demonstrated high reproducibility, balanced library representation and clear treatment-specific selection. The ADR screen identified 819 depleted and 456 enriched genes, whereas the H(2)O(2) screen identified 277 depleted and 215 enriched genes. Integrated analysis revealed both model-specific dependencies and 27 shared depleted genes across the two injury conditions, implicating stress adaptation, chromatin regulation, mitochondrial metabolism, inflammatory signaling and cytoskeletal organization as candidate processes required for podocyte survival. These genome-wide screens provide a functional framework for prioritizing genes that regulate podocyte resilience to oxidative injury and offer a resource for mechanistic studies of glomerular disease.

title: Structural basis for ITP-selective hydrolysis by a CRISPR-associated Nudix hydrolase.
authors: Wu, Wanqian; Xia, Shenglan; Li, Duo; Lin, Junchao; Cao, Chen; Kong, Jianping; Lu, Meiling; Xiao, Yibei; Li, Zhaoxing
abstract: The nucleoside diphosphates linked to moiety-X (Nudix) hydrolases are a superfamily of proteins defined by the characteristic Nudix box sequence, most of which are involved in clearing the cell of potentially deleterious metabolites and in preventing the accumulation of metabolic intermediates. The Nudix hydrolase associated with CRISPR-Cas-associated adenosine deaminases (CAAD) from Limisphaera ngatamarikiensis (LngNH) mitigates CAAD-induced toxicity by hydrolyzing ITP to IMP and pyrophosphate. Here, we determined crystal structures of LngNH in the apo form and in complex with ITP using catalytic mutants and validated key interactions by site-directed mutagenesis. The hypoxanthine of ITP is deeply buried in a hydrophobic pocket and engages a distinct hydrogen-bond network, whereas the triphosphate tail is coordinated by conserved residues and divalent metal ions. Together, these findings provide a structural framework for CAAD-linked nucleotide sanitization and suggest that CRISPR-associated Nudix hydrolases function as local self-protection modules that limit toxicity from noncanonical inosine nucleotides.IMPORTANCENucleotide quality-control enzymes protect cells from harmful metabolic by-products. Here, we characterize a CRISPR-associated nucleoside diphosphates linked to moiety-X (Nudix) hydrolase that removes ITP, a toxic noncanonical nucleotide generated during antiviral defense. Biochemical and structural analyses show how this enzyme specifically recognizes and hydrolyzes ITP while avoiding related cellular nucleotides. Our findings suggest that CRISPR-associated nucleotide deaminase systems require "self-protection" mechanisms to prevent damage from their own antiviral activities. These results expand our understanding of how bacteria maintain nucleotide homeostasis during immune responses and reveal an additional regulatory layer within CRISPR-associated defense systems. The structural framework reported here also provides a foundation for future studies of nucleotide sanitization enzymes in microbial physiology and antiviral immunity.

title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design.
abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.
